lines.say: Lesson 1: Why U S Healthcare Is Different.

lines.raw: No single national system, most people insured through a job, and very high costs.

lines.raw: In this lesson you will:
lines.say: In this lesson you will:

lines.raw: Describe how people in Nepal usually pay for healthcare.
lines.say: Describe how people in Nepal usually pay for healthcare.

lines.raw: Explain why there is no single "US health system".
lines.say: Explain why there is no single "U S health system".

lines.raw: Know the three big facts: many payers, employer cover, high cost.
lines.say: Know the three big facts: many payers, employer cover, high cost.

lines.raw: Name the five main players you will meet in this course.
lines.say: Name the five main players you will meet in this course.

lines.raw: Start with Nepal.
lines.say: Start with Nepal.

lines.raw: Before we look at the US, think about how healthcare works at home.
lines.say: Before we look at the U S, think about how healthcare works at home.

lines.raw: In Nepal you can go to a **government hospital** (like Bir Hospital or a district hospital), where you buy a cheap OPD ticket.
lines.say: In Nepal you can go to a government hospital (like Bir Hospital or a district hospital), where you buy a cheap O P D ticket.

lines.raw: Or you can go to a **private hospital** or clinic, which is usually faster but costs more.
lines.say: Or you can go to a private hospital or clinic, which is usually faster but costs more.

lines.raw: How do people pay?
lines.say: How do people pay?

lines.raw: For many families the answer is simple: **out of their own pocket**, at the counter, in cash.
lines.say: For many families the answer is simple: out of their own pocket, at the counter, in cash.

lines.raw: A large share of all health spending in Nepal is paid this way.
lines.say: A large share of all health spending in Nepal is paid this way.

lines.say: Some people have help from a scheme or an insurer:

lines.raw: Common ways people pay for care in Nepal (simplified).
lines.say: Common ways people pay for care in Nepal (simplified).

lines.raw: **Out of pocket**. Who it is for: Anyone, especially people with no cover. How it feels to the patient: Pay the full bill at the counter.
lines.say: Out of pocket. Who it is for: Anyone, especially people with no cover. How it feels to the patient: Pay the full bill at the counter.

lines.raw: **Health Insurance Board** (national health insurance). Who it is for: Families who enrol and pay a yearly premium. How it feels to the patient: Use listed health facilities, the scheme pays up to a yearly limit.
lines.say: Health Insurance Board (national health insurance). Who it is for: Families who enrol and pay a yearly premium. How it feels to the patient: Use listed health facilities, the scheme pays up to a yearly limit.

lines.raw: **Social Security Fund (SSF)**. Who it is for: Formal-sector workers whose employer is registered, like **Sita**. How it feels to the patient: Use SSF-listed hospitals, pay a share, SSF pays the rest to the hospital.
lines.say: Social Security Fund (S S F). Who it is for: Formal-sector workers whose employer is registered, like Sita. How it feels to the patient: Use S S F listed hospitals, pay a share, S S F pays the rest to the hospital.

lines.raw: **Private health insurance**. Who it is for: People whose employer buys a group policy, like **Ram**, or who buy their own. How it feels to the patient: Often pay first, then claim the money back (reimbursement).
lines.say: Private health insurance. Who it is for: People whose employer buys a group policy, like Ram, or who buy their own. How it feels to the patient: Often pay first, then claim the money back (reimbursement).

lines.raw: A note on Nepal details.
lines.say: A note on Nepal details.

lines.raw: Rules for the Health Insurance Board and SSF change from time to time.
lines.say: Rules for the Health Insurance Board and S S F change from time to time.

lines.raw: In this course we only use them as a **simple comparison**, not as an exact guide to their current rules.
lines.say: In this course we only use them as a simple comparison, not as an exact guide to their current rules.

lines.raw: Meet our people.
lines.say: Meet our people.

lines.raw: In Nepal: Ram and Sita in Kathmandu.
lines.say: In Nepal: Ram and Sita in Kathmandu.

lines.raw: With private insurance:
lines.say: With private insurance:

lines.raw: **Ram** works at a tech startup.
lines.say: Ram works at a tech startup.

lines.raw: The startup is not in SSF, but it buys **private group health insurance** for its staff.
lines.say: The startup is not in S S F, but it buys private group health insurance for its staff.

lines.raw: When Ram is sick, he pays the hospital first, keeps the bills, and sends them to the insurer to get his money back.
lines.say: When Ram is sick, he pays the hospital first, keeps the bills, and sends them to the insurer to get his money back.

lines.raw: With the Social Security Fund:
lines.say: With the Social Security Fund:

lines.raw: **Sita** is an accountant at a private company.
lines.say: Sita is an accountant at a private company.

lines.raw: Part of her salary goes to the **Social Security Fund (SSF)** every month.
lines.say: Part of her salary goes to the Social Security Fund (S S F) every month.

lines.raw: At an **SSF-listed hospital** she pays **20%** of the bill.
lines.say: At an S S F listed hospital she pays 20 percent of the bill.

lines.raw: SSF pays the other **80%** directly to the hospital.
lines.say: S S F pays the other 80 percent directly to the hospital.

lines.raw: In the US: Emily and her father Robert in Texas.
lines.say: In the U S: Emily and her father Robert in Texas.

lines.raw: **Emily Carter** is an office worker in Austin, Texas.
lines.say: Emily Carter is an office worker in Austin, Texas.

lines.raw: Her employer, **Bluebonnet Logistics** (a made-up company), gives her **health insurance**.
lines.say: Her employer, Bluebonnet Logistics (a made-up company), gives her health insurance.

lines.raw: Her husband **Daniel** and daughter **Lily** are on the same plan.
lines.say: Her husband Daniel and daughter Lily are on the same plan.

lines.raw: **Robert Carter** is Emily's father, a retired school teacher in Houston.
lines.say: Robert Carter is Emily's father, a retired school teacher in Houston.

lines.raw: He is 68 in 2025, so he is covered by **Medicare**, the government programme for people 65 and older.
lines.say: He is 68 in 2025, so he is covered by Medicare, the government programme for people 65 and older.

lines.raw: He gets his Medicare through a private plan called **Gulf Coast Advantage (HMO)** (made up).
lines.say: He gets his Medicare through a private plan called Gulf Coast Advantage (H M O) (made up).

lines.raw: Two people in one family, two very different sources of cover.
lines.say: Two people in one family, two very different sources of cover.

lines.raw: That is normal in the US.
lines.say: That is normal in the U S.

lines.raw: Big fact 1: there is no single US system.
lines.say: Big fact 1: there is no single U S system.

scenes.section: Big fact 1: there is no single US system

lines.raw: Many countries have one main national system.
lines.say: Many countries have one main national system.

lines.raw: The UK, for example, has the NHS, paid for by taxes.
lines.say: The U K, for example, has the N H S, paid for by taxes.

lines.raw: The US does not.
lines.say: The U S does not.

lines.raw: Instead it has **many separate systems** side by side: private insurance companies, employer plans, and several government programmes, each with its own rules.
lines.say: Instead it has many separate systems side by side: private insurance companies, employer plans, and several government programmes, each with its own rules.

scenes.section: Big fact 1: there is no single US system

lines.raw: Think of buses in Kathmandu.
lines.say: Think of buses in Kathmandu.

lines.raw: There is no single bus company in Kathmandu.
lines.say: There is no single bus company in Kathmandu.

lines.raw: Sajha Yatayat, private micro buses, tempos and many small operators all run on the same roads, each with its own fares and routes.
lines.say: Sajha Yatayat, private micro buses, tempos and many small operators all run on the same roads, each with its own fares and routes.

lines.raw: US healthcare is similar: many **payers** run on the same "roads" (the same hospitals and doctors), each with its own prices and rules.
lines.say: U S healthcare is similar: many payers run on the same "roads" (the same hospitals and doctors), each with its own prices and rules.

lines.raw: Big fact 2: most people get insurance through a job.
lines.say: Big fact 2: most people get insurance through a job.

scenes.section: Big fact 2: most people get insurance through a job

lines.raw: In the US, the most common way to get health insurance is through an **employer**.
lines.say: In the U S, the most common way to get health insurance is through an employer.

lines.raw: About half of all Americans are covered this way.
lines.say: About half of all Americans are covered this way.

lines.raw: The employer chooses an insurance plan, pays most of the cost, and the worker pays the rest from each paycheck.
lines.say: The employer chooses an insurance plan, pays most of the cost, and the worker pays the rest from each paycheck.

lines.raw: This is exactly like **Ram's** startup buying a group policy, but in the US it is the normal case, not the exception.
lines.say: This is exactly like Ram's startup buying a group policy, but in the U S it is the normal case, not the exception.

scenes.section: Big fact 2: most people get insurance through a job

lines.raw: Lose the job, lose the insurance.
lines.say: Lose the job, lose the insurance.

lines.raw: Because cover is tied to a job, losing a job can mean losing health insurance.
lines.say: Because cover is tied to a job, losing a job can mean losing health insurance.

lines.raw: Emily's husband **Daniel** lost his job in 2025, and with it his insurance.
lines.say: Emily's husband Daniel lost his job in 2025, and with it his insurance.

lines.raw: On **1 July 2025** he joined Emily's plan instead.
lines.say: On 1 July 2025 he joined Emily's plan instead.

lines.say: Big fact 3: care is very expensive.

scenes.section: Big fact 3: care is very expensive

lines.raw: US health spending in 2023 (source: CMS, rounded).
lines.say: U S health spending in 2023 (source: C M S, rounded).

lines.raw: Total spent in one year. Amount: About **$4.9 trillion**. To picture it: More than 100 times Nepal's whole economy.
lines.say: Total spent in one year. Amount: About 4.9 trillion dollars. To picture it: More than 100 times Nepal's whole economy.

lines.raw: Share of the US economy. Amount: About **17.6%**. To picture it: Roughly **$1 of every $6** spent in the US.
lines.say: Share of the U S economy. Amount: About 17.6 percent. To picture it: Roughly 1 dollar of every 6 dollars spent in the U S.

lines.raw: Spent per person. Amount: About **$14,570**. To picture it: Roughly **Rs 20 lakh** per person, every year.
lines.say: Spent per person. Amount: About 14570 dollars. To picture it: Roughly Rs 20 lakh per person, every year.

scenes.section: Big fact 3: care is very expensive

lines.raw: A simple doctor visit can cost **$150** or more, and a short hospital stay can cost many thousands of dollars.
lines.say: A simple doctor visit can cost 150 dollars or more, and a short hospital stay can cost many thousands of dollars.

lines.raw: Without insurance, one surgery can wipe out a family's savings.
lines.say: Without insurance, one surgery can wipe out a family's savings.

lines.raw: That is why almost everything in US healthcare revolves around **who pays**.
lines.say: That is why almost everything in U S healthcare revolves around who pays.

lines.raw: The big idea.
lines.say: The big idea.

lines.raw: In Nepal, the patient is often also the payer.
lines.say: In Nepal, the patient is often also the payer.

lines.raw: In the US, the patient, the provider and the payer are almost always **three different parties**.
lines.say: In the U S, the patient, the provider and the payer are almost always three different parties.

lines.raw: Most of US healthcare (and most of its data) is about these three talking to each other.
